messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

## Navigation policy

Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:

Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:

- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)

### **1. Temporal Sequence Understanding**

The video opens with a **short introductory clip (0:00–0:04)** showing a sea otter floating on its back in water, looking directly at the camera. This appears to be a generic “outro” or channel branding sequence (with text “Thanks for watching… Subscribe here”), likely not part of the main footage but used as a lead-in/out.

Then, from **0:05 onward**, the primary footage begins — set in a polar environment (Antarctica), featuring:
- A group of fluffy, greyish juvenile penguins (Emperor penguin chicks).

- In the background, more penguins and ice features are visible.

The video ends with a **blue outro screen (1:56–1:58)** displaying production credits and social media handles.

Thus, the core biological content occurs from **00:05 to 01:55**, with three distinct animal species clearly visible.

---

### **2. Motion and Action Analysis**

#### **Sea Otter (*Enhydra lutris*)**
- **Time**: 0:00–0:04 (intro only)
- **Behavior**: Floating on back, front paws raised, looking into camera; then submerges head underwater.
- **Note**: This is likely stock footage unrelated to the Antarctic scenes; no other otters appear.

#### **Emperor Penguin Chicks (*Aptenodytes forsteri*)**
- **Time**: From 0:05 onward, dominant subject.
- **Appearance**: Fluffy, grey downy plumage; black heads with white facial patches; large eyes; short beaks; no adult coloration yet (no yellow-orange ear patches).
- **Count**: In various shots, group sizes range from ~9 to ~15 individuals. At 1:47–1:50, a wide shot shows ~20+ chicks huddled together, plus some scattered individuals.
- **Behavior**:
  - Huddling tightly for warmth (typical crèche behavior).
  - Reacting defensively to the petrel: flapping flippers, squawking, leaning away, some falling over.
  - One chick falls and struggles to stand (0:21–0:23).
  - Some vocalize (open beaks, head tilting upward) — likely alarm calls.
  - When the Adélie penguin walks by (1:21–1:26), chicks remain mostly still but watch it pass.

#### **Southern Giant Petrel (*Macronectes giganteus*)**
- **Time**: Appears repeatedly from 0:09 onward.
- **Identification**:
  - Large, bulky seabird (~90 cm long, wingspan ~2 m).
  - Dark brown plumage (juveniles are uniformly dark brown; adults have white-brown mottling, but this individual appears juvenile or subadult).
  - Distinctive pale yellowish-green bill with a hooked tip and tubular nostrils (visible in close-ups at 0:35, 1:12, 1:37).
  - Walks awkwardly on snow with wings partially extended for balance.
- **Behavior**:
  - Approaches penguin crèche multiple times.
  - Lunges at chicks (0:26–0:34): spreads wings, pecks, attempts to grab one chick — classic predation/scavenging behavior.
  - Retreats after being mobbed or when chicks react aggressively (flipping flippers, hissing).
  - At 0:49, seen on bare ground (melted snow/ice), suggesting variable terrain.

#### **Adélie Penguin (*Pygoscelis adeliae*)**
- **Time**: 1:21–1:26 (brief appearance); also visible in background at 1:47–1:50.
- **Identification**:
  - Smaller than Emperor penguins (~70 cm tall).
  - Classic black-and-white tuxedo plumage.
  - Distinctive white eye-ring and black head.
  - Shorter beak, upright gait.
- **Behavior**:
  - Walks briskly across snow/ice, passing near the crèche.
  - Does not interact with chicks or petrel — appears indifferent.
- **Count**: At least **one clearly visible individual** walking past; additional indistinct figures in background at 1:47–1:50 suggest possibly 2–3 more, but not reliably countable.

#### **Other Background Penguins**
- In wide shots (e.g., 1:47–1:50, 1:54), many penguins are visible in the distance:
  - Some are clearly **adult Emperor Penguins** (black backs, yellow-orange neck patches).
  - Others are likely **chicks** (grey downy) or possibly **juvenile Emperors** molting.
  - No clear evidence of other *species* besides Emperor and Adélie.
- No seals, whales, skuas, or other birds are definitively identifiable.

---

- **Location**: Antarctic sea ice, near an ice cliff/glacier (visible at 0:05, 1:47, 1:54). Snow-covered, windy (snow drift visible at 1:32–1:36).
- **Season**: Likely late austral summer (December–February), when Emperor penguin chicks are old enough to form crèches but not yet fledged (~3–5 months old). Southern Giant Petrels are common scavengers/predators during this period.
- **Ecological Interaction**: The video captures a natural predator–prey (or scavenger–vulnerable young) interaction. Giant petrels are known to prey on weak or isolated Emperor penguin chicks. The chicks’ defensive huddling and vocalizations are typical anti-predator behaviors.

No plants or fungi are visible — the environment is abiotic (ice, snow, rock). No algae or microbial mats are discernible.

Individual identification is difficult due to similarity, but movements suggest continuity (e.g., same chick falls at 0:21 and reappears later).
- **Southern Giant Petrel**: One individual tracked throughout — same plumage, bill shape, behavior. No duplication.
- **Adélie Penguin**: One clearly tracked walking past; others in background are unconfirmed.

{
  "success": true,
  "message": "Let’s conduct a comprehensive analysis of all visible biological entities in the video, following the requested steps.

---

### **1. Temporal Sequence Understanding**

The video opens with a **short introductory clip (0:00–0:04)** showing a sea otter floating on its back in water, looking directly at the camera. This appears to be a generic “outro” or channel branding sequence (with text “Thanks for watching… Subscribe here”), likely not part of the main footage but used as a lead-in/out.

Then, from **0:05 onward**, the primary footage begins — set in a polar environment (Antarctica), featuring:
- A group of fluffy, greyish juvenile penguins (Emperor penguin chicks).
- An adult seabird interacting with them — identified as a **Southern Giant Petrel** (*Macronectes giganteus*).
- Later, an adult **Adélie Penguin** (*Pygoscelis adeliae*) walks through the scene.
- In the background, more penguins and ice features are visible.

The video ends with a **blue outro screen (1:56–1:58)** displaying production credits and social media handles.

Thus, the core biological content occurs from **00:05 to 01:55**, with three distinct animal species clearly visible.

---

### **2. Motion and Action Analysis**

#### **Sea Otter (*Enhydra lutris*)**
- **Time**: 0:00–0:04 (intro only)
- **Behavior**: Floating on back, front paws raised, looking into camera; then submerges head underwater.
- **Note**: This is likely stock footage unrelated to the Antarctic scenes; no other otters appear.

#### **Emperor Penguin Chicks (*Aptenodytes forsteri*)**
- **Time**: From 0:05 onward, dominant subject.
- **Appearance**: Fluffy, grey downy plumage; black heads with white facial patches; large eyes; short beaks; no adult coloration yet (no yellow-orange ear patches).
- **Count**: In various shots, group sizes range from ~9 to ~15 individuals. At 1:47–1:50, a wide shot shows ~20+ chicks huddled together, plus some scattered individuals.
- **Behavior**:
  - Huddling tightly for warmth (typical crèche behavior).
  - Reacting defensively to the petrel: flapping flippers, squawking, leaning away, some falling over.
  - One chick falls and struggles to stand (0:21–0:23).
  - Some vocalize (open beaks, head tilting upward) — likely alarm calls.
  - When the Adélie penguin walks by (1:21–1:26), chicks remain mostly still but watch it pass.

#### **Southern Giant Petrel (*Macronectes giganteus*)**
- **Time**: Appears repeatedly from 0:09 onward.
- **Identification**:
  - Large, bulky seabird (~90 cm long, wingspan ~2 m).
  - Dark brown plumage (juveniles are uniformly dark brown; adults have white-brown mottling, but this individual appears juvenile or subadult).
  - Distinctive pale yellowish-green bill with a hooked tip and tubular nostrils (visible in close-ups at 0:35, 1:12, 1:37).
  - Walks awkwardly on snow with wings partially extended for balance.
- **Behavior**:
  - Approaches penguin crèche multiple times.
  - Lunges at chicks (0:26–0:34): spreads wings, pecks, attempts to grab one chick — classic predation/scavenging behavior.
  - Retreats after being mobbed or when chicks react aggressively (flipping flippers, hissing).
  - At 0:49, seen on bare ground (melted snow/ice), suggesting variable terrain.
  - Eventually sits calmly (1:07–1:11, 1:16–1:20), observing the group — possibly assessing opportunity or resting.
  - Flies off at 1:44–1:45 (low flight over snow).
- **Count**: Only **one** individual is consistently shown throughout the interaction sequences. No evidence of others (though distant birds may be present in wide shots, they’re too indistinct).

#### **Adélie Penguin (*Pygoscelis adeliae*)**
- **Time**: 1:21–1:26 (brief appearance); also visible in background at 1:47–1:50.
- **Identification**:
  - Smaller than Emperor penguins (~70 cm tall).
  - Classic black-and-white tuxedo plumage.
  - Distinctive white eye-ring and black head.
  - Shorter beak, upright gait.
- **Behavior**:
  - Walks briskly across snow/ice, passing near the crèche.
  - Does not interact with chicks or petrel — appears indifferent.
- **Count**: At least **one clearly visible individual** walking past; additional indistinct figures in background at 1:47–1:50 suggest possibly 2–3 more, but not reliably countable.

#### **Other Background Penguins**
- In wide shots (e.g., 1:47–1:50, 1:54), many penguins are visible in the distance:
  - Some are clearly **adult Emperor Penguins** (black backs, yellow-orange neck patches).
  - Others are likely **chicks** (grey downy) or possibly **juvenile Emperors** molting.
  - No clear evidence of other *species* besides Emperor and Adélie.
- No seals, whales, skuas, or other birds are definitively identifiable.

---

### **3. Scene Context Interpretation**

- **Location**: Antarctic sea ice, near an ice cliff/glacier (visible at 0:05, 1:47, 1:54). Snow-covered, windy (snow drift visible at 1:32–1:36).
- **Season**: Likely late austral summer (December–February), when Emperor penguin chicks are old enough to form crèches but not yet fledged (~3–5 months old). Southern Giant Petrels are common scavengers/predators during this period.
- **Ecological Interaction**: The video captures a natural predator–prey (or scavenger–vulnerable young) interaction. Giant petrels are known to prey on weak or isolated Emperor penguin chicks. The chicks’ defensive huddling and vocalizations are typical anti-predator behaviors.

No plants or fungi are visible — the environment is abiotic (ice, snow, rock). No algae or microbial mats are discernible.

---

### **4. Object and Person Tracking**

- **Sea Otter**: Single individual, only in intro (0:00–0:04). Not part of main ecological scene.
- **Emperor Penguin Chicks**: Same cohort tracked across scenes. Estimated **12–20 individuals** total across frames, with ~10–12 consistently in medium/close shots. Individual identification is difficult due to similarity, but movements suggest continuity (e.g., same chick falls at 0:21 and reappears later).
- **Southern Giant Petrel**: One individual tracked throughout — same plumage, bill shape, behavior. No duplication.
- **Adélie Penguin**: One clearly tracked walking past; others in background are unconfirmed.

No humans, equipment, or artificial objects (except watermark/logo overlays) are visible in the field footage.

---

## ✅ Final Species Inventory & Summary

| # | Species | Scientific Name | Life Stage | Approx. Count | Notes |
|---|---------|------------------|------------|---------------|-------|
| 1 | Sea Otter | *Enhydra lutris* | Adult | 1 | Intro only; not ecologically linked to main footage. |
| 2 | Emperor Penguin | *Aptenodytes forsteri* | Juvenile (chicks, downy) | 12–20 (observable) | Primary subjects; form crèche; exhibit anti-predator behavior. |
| 3 | Southern Giant Petrel | *Macronectes giganteus* | Juvenile/subadult | 1 | Repeated interactions with chicks; attempted predation. |
| 4 | Adélie Penguin | *Pygoscelis adeliae* | Adult | ≥1 (1 confirmed, 1–2 possible in bg) | Brief passerby; no interaction. |

### 🚫 Absent / Not Identified:
- No skuas (though often associate with penguin colonies — none clearly visible).
- No Weddell seals, leopard seals, or other mammals.
- No vascular plants, mosses, lichens, or phytoplankton visible.
- No insects or invertebrates.

---

## Conclusion

The video clearly documents **four distinct animal species**, though only **three** are ecologically interacting in the Antarctic setting (Emperor penguin chicks, Southern Giant Petrel, and Adélie penguin). The sea otter is a non-contextual intro element.

The most significant biological observation is the natural predatory/scavenging behavior of the Southern Giant Petrel toward vulnerable Emperor penguin chicks — a well-documented but rarely captured interaction in such detail.

function.description:

        This tool uses Tesseract OCR to extract text content from images,
        with optional preprocessing to improve recognition accuracy.

        Args:
            file_path: Path to the image file
            language: OCR language for better recognition
            preprocess: Whether to enhance image for OCR

### **1. Temporal Sequence Understanding**

The video opens with a **short introductory clip (0:00–0:04)** showing a sea otter floating on its back in water, looking directly at the camera. The video ends with a **blue outro screen (1:56–1:58)** displaying production credits and social media handles.

Thus, the core biological content occurs from **00:05 to 01:55**, with three distinct animal species clearly visible.

### **2. Motion and Action Analysis**

#### **Sea Otter (*Enhydra lutris*)**
- **Time**: 0:00–0:04 (intro only)
- **Behavior**: Floating on back, front paws raised, looking into camera; then submerges head underwater.
- **Note**: This is likely stock footage unrelated to the Antarctic scenes; no other otters appear.

#### **Emperor Penguin Chicks (*Aptenodytes forsteri*)**
- **Time**: From 0:05 onward, dominant subject.
- **Appearance**: Fluffy, grey downy plumage; black heads with white facial patches; large eyes; short beaks; no adult coloration yet (no yellow-orange ear patches).

- **Behavior**:

  - Some vocalize (open beaks, head tilting upward) — likely alarm calls.
  - When the Adélie penguin walks by (1:21–1:26), chicks remain mostly still but watch it pass.

#### **Southern Giant Petrel (*Macronectes giganteus*)**
- **Time**: Appears repeatedly from 0:09 onward.
- **Identification**:
  - Large, bulky seabird (~90 cm long, wingspan ~2 m).
  - Dark brown plumage (juveniles are uniformly dark brown; adults have white-brown mottling, but this individual appears juvenile or subadult).
  - Distinctive pale yellowish-green bill with a hooked tip and tubular nostrils (visible in close-ups at 0:35, 1:12, 1:37).
  - Walks awkwardly on snow with wings partially extended for balance.
- **Behavior**:
  - Approaches penguin crèche multiple times.

  - Retreats after being mobbed or when chicks react aggressively (flipping flippers, hissing).
  - At 0:49, seen on bare ground (melted snow/ice), suggesting variable terrain.

  - Flies off at 1:44–1:45 (low flight over snow).
- **Count**: Only **one** individual is consistently shown throughout the interaction sequences. No evidence of others (though distant birds may be present in wide shots, they’re too indistinct).

#### **Adélie Penguin (*Pygoscelis adeliae*)**
- **Time**: 1:21–1:26 (brief appearance); also visible in background at 1:47–1:50.
- **Identification**:
  - Smaller than Emperor penguins (~70 cm tall).
  - Classic black-and-white tuxedo plumage.

  - Shorter beak, upright gait.
- **Behavior**:
  - Walks briskly across snow/ice, passing near the crèche.
  - Does not interact with chicks or petrel — appears indifferent.
- **Count**: At least **one clearly visible individual** walking past; additional indistinct figures in background at 1:47–1:50 suggest possibly 2–3 more, but not reliably countable.

#### **Other Background Penguins**

  - No clear evidence of other *species* besides Emperor and Adélie.
- No seals, whales, skuas, or other birds are definitively identifiable.

---

- **Location**: Antarctic sea ice, near an ice cliff/glacier (visible at 0:05, 1:47, 1:54). Snow-covered, windy (snow drift visible at 1:32–1:36).
- **Season**: Likely late austral summer (December–February), when Emperor penguin chicks are old enough to form crèches but not yet fledged (~3–5 months old). Southern Giant Petrels are common scavengers/predators during this period.
- **Ecological Interaction**: The video captures a natural predator–prey (or scavenger–vulnerable young) interaction. Giant petrels are known to prey on weak or isolated Emperor penguin chicks. The chicks’ defensive huddling and vocalizations are typical anti-predator behaviors.

No plants or fungi are visible — the environment is abiotic (ice, snow, rock). No algae or microbial mats are discernible.

- **Emperor Penguin Chicks**: Same cohort tracked across scenes. Estimated **12–20 individuals** total across frames, with ~10–12 consistently in medium/close shots. Individual identification is difficult due to similarity, but movements suggest continuity (e.g., same chick falls at 0:21 and reappears later).
- **Southern Giant Petrel**: One individual tracked throughout — same plumage, bill shape, behavior. No duplication.

### **1. Temporal Sequence Understanding**

The video opens with a **short introductory clip (0:00–0:04)** showing a sea otter floating on its back in water, looking directly at the camera. The video ends with a **blue outro screen (1:56–1:58)** displaying production credits and social media handles.

Thus, the core biological content occurs from **00:05 to 01:55**, with three distinct animal species clearly visible.

### **2. Motion and Action Analysis**

#### **Sea Otter (*Enhydra lutris*)**
- **Time**: 0:00–0:04 (intro only)
- **Behavior**: Floating on back, front paws raised, looking into camera; then submerges head underwater.
- **Note**: This is likely stock footage unrelated to the Antarctic scenes; no other otters appear.

- **Time**: From 0:05 onward, dominant subject.
- **Appearance**: Fluffy, grey downy plumage; black heads with white facial patches; large eyes; short beaks; no adult coloration yet (no yellow-orange ear patches).

  - Some vocalize (open beaks, head tilting upward) — likely alarm calls.
  - When the Adélie penguin walks by (1:21–1:26), chicks remain mostly still but watch it pass.

#### **Southern Giant Petrel (*Macronectes giganteus*)**
- **Time**: Appears repeatedly from 0:09 onward.
- **Identification**:
  - Large, bulky seabird (~90 cm long, wingspan ~2 m).
  - Dark brown plumage (juveniles are uniformly dark brown; adults have white-brown mottling, but this individual appears juvenile or subadult).
  - Distinctive pale yellowish-green bill with a hooked tip and tubular nostrils (visible in close-ups at 0:35, 1:12, 1:37).

#### **Adélie Penguin (*Pygoscelis adeliae*)**
- **Time**: 1:21–1:26 (brief appearance); also visible in background at 1:47–1:50.
- **Identification**:
  - Smaller than Emperor penguins (~70 cm tall).

- **Location**: Antarctic sea ice, near an ice cliff/glacier (visible at 0:05, 1:47, 1:54). Snow-covered, windy (snow drift visible at 1:32–1:36).
- **Season**: Likely late austral summer (December–February), when Emperor penguin chicks are old enough to form crèches but not yet fledged (~3–5 months old). Southern Giant Petrels are common scavengers/predators during this period.
- **Ecological Interaction**: The video captures a natural predator–prey (or scavenger–vulnerable young) interaction. Giant petrels are known to prey on weak or isolated Emperor penguin chicks. The chicks’ defensive huddling and vocalizations are typical anti-predator behaviors.

No plants or fungi are visible — the environment is abiotic (ice, snow, rock). No algae or microbial mats are discernible.

Individual identification is difficult due to similarity, but movements suggest continuity (e.g., same chick falls at 0:21 and reappears later).
- **Southern Giant Petrel**: One individual tracked throughout — same plumage, bill shape, behavior. No duplication.

        This tool provides comprehensive video analysis capabilities including:
        - Content understanding and description
        - Object and scene detection
        - Action and movement analysis
        - Temporal event tracking
        - Question-answering about video content
        - Parallel processing for faster analysis

        Args:
            video_url: Path or URL to the video file
            question: Specific question or analysis task
            sample_rate: Frame sampling rate for analysis
            start_time: Start time of the video segment in seconds
            end_time: End time of the video segment in seconds
            output_format: Format for the response output
            max_workers: Maximum number of parallel workers

        Returns:
            ActionResponse with video analysis results and metadata

function.name: mcp_extract_keyframes
function.description:
Extract key frames around a target time with scene detection.

        This tool provides keyframe extraction with:
        - Scene detection for significant frame changes
        - Configurable time windows
        - Automatic output directory management
        - LLM-optimized result formatting

        Args:
            video_path: The input video filepath or URL
            target_time: Specific time point (in seconds) to extract frames around
            window_size: Time window (in seconds) centered on target_time
            cleanup: Whether to delete the original video file after processing
            output_dir: Directory where extracted frames will be saved
            output_format: Format for the response output

        Returns:
            ActionResponse with keyframe extraction results and metadata

video_path.title: Video Path

target_time.description: The specific time point for extraction (in seconds), centered within the window_size.

{
  "success": true,
  "message": "Let’s conduct a comprehensive analysis of all visible biological entities in the video, following the requested steps.

---

### **1. Temporal Sequence Understanding**

The video opens with a **short introductory clip (0:00–0:04)** showing a sea otter floating on its back in water, looking directly at the camera. This appears to be a generic “outro” or channel branding sequence (with text “Thanks for watching… Subscribe here”), likely not part of the main footage but used as a lead-in/out.

Then, from **0:05 onward**, the primary footage begins — set in a polar environment (Antarctica), featuring:
- A group of fluffy, greyish juvenile penguins (Emperor penguin chicks).
- An adult seabird interacting with them — identified as a **Southern Giant Petrel** (*Macronectes giganteus*).
- Later, an adult **Adélie Penguin** (*Pygoscelis adeliae*) walks through the scene.
- In the background, more penguins and ice features are visible.

The video ends with a **blue outro screen (1:56–1:58)** displaying production credits and social media handles.

Thus, the core biological content occurs from **00:05 to 01:55**, with three distinct animal species clearly visible.

---

### **2. Motion and Action Analysis**

#### **Sea Otter (*Enhydra lutris*)**
- **Time**: 0:00–0:04 (intro only)
- **Behavior**: Floating on back, front paws raised, looking into camera; then submerges head underwater.
- **Note**: This is likely stock footage unrelated to the Antarctic scenes; no other otters appear.

#### **Emperor Penguin Chicks (*Aptenodytes forsteri*)**
- **Time**: From 0:05 onward, dominant subject.
- **Appearance**: Fluffy, grey downy plumage; black heads with white facial patches; large eyes; short beaks; no adult coloration yet (no yellow-orange ear patches).
- **Count**: In various shots, group sizes range from ~9 to ~15 individuals. At 1:47–1:50, a wide shot shows ~20+ chicks huddled together, plus some scattered individuals.
- **Behavior**:
  - Huddling tightly for warmth (typical crèche behavior).
  - Reacting defensively to the petrel: flapping flippers, squawking, leaning away, some falling over.
  - One chick falls and struggles to stand (0:21–0:23).
  - Some vocalize (open beaks, head tilting upward) — likely alarm calls.
  - When the Adélie penguin walks by (1:21–1:26), chicks remain mostly still but watch it pass.

#### **Southern Giant Petrel (*Macronectes giganteus*)**
- **Time**: Appears repeatedly from 0:09 onward.
- **Identification**:
  - Large, bulky seabird (~90 cm long, wingspan ~2 m).
  - Dark brown plumage (juveniles are uniformly dark brown; adults have white-brown mottling, but this individual appears juvenile or subadult).
  - Distinctive pale yellowish-green bill with a hooked tip and tubular nostrils (visible in close-ups at 0:35, 1:12, 1:37).
  - Walks awkwardly on snow with wings partially extended for balance.
- **Behavior**:
  - Approaches penguin crèche multiple times.
  - Lunges at chicks (0:26–0:34): spreads wings, pecks, attempts to grab one chick — classic predation/scavenging behavior.
  - Retreats after being mobbed or when chicks react aggressively (flipping flippers, hissing).
  - At 0:49, seen on bare ground (melted snow/ice), suggesting variable terrain.
  - Eventually sits calmly (1:07–1:11, 1:16–1:20), observing the group — possibly assessing opportunity or resting.
  - Flies off at 1:44–1:45 (low flight over snow).
- **Count**: Only **one** individual is consistently shown throughout the interaction sequences. No evidence of others (though distant birds may be present in wide shots, they’re too indistinct).

#### **Adélie Penguin (*Pygoscelis adeliae*)**
- **Time**: 1:21–1:26 (brief appearance); also visible in background at 1:47–1:50.
- **Identification**:
  - Smaller than Emperor penguins (~70 cm tall).
  - Classic black-and-white tuxedo plumage.
  - Distinctive white eye-ring and black head.
  - Shorter beak, upright gait.
- **Behavior**:
  - Walks briskly across snow/ice, passing near the crèche.
  - Does not interact with chicks or petrel — appears indifferent.
- **Count**: At least **one clearly visible individual** walking past; additional indistinct figures in background at 1:47–1:50 suggest possibly 2–3 more, but not reliably countable.

#### **Other Background Penguins**
- In wide shots (e.g., 1:47–1:50, 1:54), many penguins are visible in the distance:
  - Some are clearly **adult Emperor Penguins** (black backs, yellow-orange neck patches).
  - Others are likely **chicks** (grey downy) or possibly **juvenile Emperors** molting.
  - No clear evidence of other *species* besides Emperor and Adélie.
- No seals, whales, skuas, or other birds are definitively identifiable.

---

### **3. Scene Context Interpretation**

- **Location**: Antarctic sea ice, near an ice cliff/glacier (visible at 0:05, 1:47, 1:54). Snow-covered, windy (snow drift visible at 1:32–1:36).
- **Season**: Likely late austral summer (December–February), when Emperor penguin chicks are old enough to form crèches but not yet fledged (~3–5 months old). Southern Giant Petrels are common scavengers/predators during this period.
- **Ecological Interaction**: The video captures a natural predator–prey (or scavenger–vulnerable young) interaction. Giant petrels are known to prey on weak or isolated Emperor penguin chicks. The chicks’ defensive huddling and vocalizations are typical anti-predator behaviors.

No plants or fungi are visible — the environment is abiotic (ice, snow, rock). No algae or microbial mats are discernible.

---

### **4. Object and Person Tracking**

- **Sea Otter**: Single individual, only in intro (0:00–0:04). Not part of main ecological scene.
- **Emperor Penguin Chicks**: Same cohort tracked across scenes. Estimated **12–20 individuals** total across frames, with ~10–12 consistently in medium/close shots. Individual identification is difficult due to similarity, but movements suggest continuity (e.g., same chick falls at 0:21 and reappears later).
- **Southern Giant Petrel**: One individual tracked throughout — same plumage, bill shape, behavior. No duplication.
- **Adélie Penguin**: One clearly tracked walking past; others in background are unconfirmed.

No humans, equipment, or artificial objects (except watermark/logo overlays) are visible in the field footage.

---

## ✅ Final Species Inventory & Summary

| # | Species | Scientific Name | Life Stage | Approx. Count | Notes |
|---|---------|------------------|------------|---------------|-------|
| 1 | Sea Otter | *Enhydra lutris* | Adult | 1 | Intro only; not ecologically linked to main footage. |
| 2 | Emperor Penguin | *Aptenodytes forsteri* | Juvenile (chicks, downy) | 12–20 (observable) | Primary subjects; form crèche; exhibit anti-predator behavior. |
| 3 | Southern Giant Petrel | *Macronectes giganteus* | Juvenile/subadult | 1 | Repeated interactions with chicks; attempted predation. |
| 4 | Adélie Penguin | *Pygoscelis adeliae* | Adult | ≥1 (1 confirmed, 1–2 possible in bg) | Brief passerby; no interaction. |

### 🚫 Absent / Not Identified:
- No skuas (though often associate with penguin colonies — none clearly visible).
- No Weddell seals, leopard seals, or other mammals.
- No vascular plants, mosses, lichens, or phytoplankton visible.
- No insects or invertebrates.

---

## Conclusion

The video clearly documents **four distinct animal species**, though only **three** are ecologically interacting in the Antarctic setting (Emperor penguin chicks, Southern Giant Petrel, and Adélie penguin). The sea otter is a non-contextual intro element.

The most significant biological observation is the natural predatory/scavenging behavior of the Southern Giant Petrel toward vulnerable Emperor penguin chicks — a well-documented but rarely captured interaction in such detail.

All identifications are based on morphology, behavior, habitat, and geographic plausibility (Antarctic region). No misidentifications (e.g., mistaking petrel for skua) are evident — the bill shape, size, and plumage confirm *Macronectes giganteus*.",

{
  "success": true,
  "message": "Let’s conduct a comprehensive analysis of all visible biological entities in the video, following the requested steps.

---

### **1. Temporal Sequence Understanding**

The video opens with a **short introductory clip (0:00–0:04)** showing a sea otter floating on its back in water, looking directly at the camera. This appears to be a generic “outro” or channel branding sequence (with text “Thanks for watching… Subscribe here”), likely not part of the main footage but used as a lead-in/out.

Then, from **0:05 onward**, the primary footage begins — set in a polar environment (Antarctica), featuring:
- A group of fluffy, greyish juvenile penguins (Emperor penguin chicks).
- An adult seabird interacting with them — identified as a **Southern Giant Petrel** (*Macronectes giganteus*).
- Later, an adult **Adélie Penguin** (*Pygoscelis adeliae*) walks through the scene.
- In the background, more penguins and ice features are visible.

The video ends with a **blue outro screen (1:56–1:58)** displaying production credits and social media handles.

Thus, the core biological content occurs from **00:05 to 01:55**, with three distinct animal species clearly visible.

---

### **2. Motion and Action Analysis**

#### **Sea Otter (*Enhydra lutris*)**
- **Time**: 0:00–0:04 (intro only)
- **Behavior**: Floating on back, front paws raised, looking into camera; then submerges head underwater.
- **Note**: This is likely stock footage unrelated to the Antarctic scenes; no other otters appear.

#### **Emperor Penguin Chicks (*Aptenodytes forsteri*)**
- **Time**: From 0:05 onward, dominant subject.
- **Appearance**: Fluffy, grey downy plumage; black heads with white facial patches; large eyes; short beaks; no adult coloration yet (no yellow-orange ear patches).
- **Count**: In various shots, group sizes range from ~9 to ~15 individuals. At 1:47–1:50, a wide shot shows ~20+ chicks huddled together, plus some scattered individuals.
- **Behavior**:
  - Huddling tightly for warmth (typical crèche behavior).
  - Reacting defensively to the petrel: flapping flippers, squawking, leaning away, some falling over.
  - One chick falls and struggles to stand (0:21–0:23).
  - Some vocalize (open beaks, head tilting upward) — likely alarm calls.
  - When the Adélie penguin walks by (1:21–1:26), chicks remain mostly still but watch it pass.

#### **Southern Giant Petrel (*Macronectes giganteus*)**
- **Time**: Appears repeatedly from 0:09 onward.
- **Identification**:
  - Large, bulky seabird (~90 cm long, wingspan ~2 m).
  - Dark brown plumage (juveniles are uniformly dark brown; adults have white-brown mottling, but this individual appears juvenile or subadult).
  - Distinctive pale yellowish-green bill with a hooked tip and tubular nostrils (visible in close-ups at 0:35, 1:12, 1:37).
  - Walks awkwardly on snow with wings partially extended for balance.
- **Behavior**:
  - Approaches penguin crèche multiple times.
  - Lunges at chicks (0:26–0:34): spreads wings, pecks, attempts to grab one chick — classic predation/scavenging behavior.
  - Retreats after being mobbed or when chicks react aggressively (flipping flippers, hissing).
  - At 0:49, seen on bare ground (melted snow/ice), suggesting variable terrain.
  - Eventually sits calmly (1:07–1:11, 1:16–1:20), observing the group — possibly assessing opportunity or resting.
  - Flies off at 1:44–1:45 (low flight over snow).
- **Count**: Only **one** individual is consistently shown throughout the interaction sequences. No evidence of others (though distant birds may be present in wide shots, they’re too indistinct).

#### **Adélie Penguin (*Pygoscelis adeliae*)**
- **Time**: 1:21–1:26 (brief appearance); also visible in background at 1:47–1:50.
- **Identification**:
  - Smaller than Emperor penguins (~70 cm tall).
  - Classic black-and-white tuxedo plumage.
  - Distinctive white eye-ring and black head.
  - Shorter beak, upright gait.
- **Behavior**:
  - Walks briskly across snow/ice, passing near the crèche.
  - Does not interact with chicks or petrel — appears indifferent.
- **Count**: At least **one clearly visible individual** walking past; additional indistinct figures in background at 1:47–1:50 suggest possibly 2–3 more, but not reliably countable.

#### **Other Background Penguins**
- In wide shots (e.g., 1:47–1:50, 1:54), many penguins are visible in the distance:
  - Some are clearly **adult Emperor Penguins** (black backs, yellow-orange neck patches).
  - Others are likely **chicks** (grey downy) or possibly **juvenile Emperors** molting.
  - No clear evidence of other *species* besides Emperor and Adélie.
- No seals, whales, skuas, or other birds are definitively identifiable.

---

### **3. Scene Context Interpretation**

- **Location**: Antarctic sea ice, near an ice cliff/glacier (visible at 0:05, 1:47, 1:54). Snow-covered, windy (snow drift visible at 1:32–1:36).
- **Season**: Likely late austral summer (December–February), when Emperor penguin chicks are old enough to form crèches but not yet fledged (~3–5 months old). Southern Giant Petrels are common scavengers/predators during this period.
- **Ecological Interaction**: The video captures a natural predator–prey (or scavenger–vulnerable young) interaction. Giant petrels are known to prey on weak or isolated Emperor penguin chicks. The chicks’ defensive huddling and vocalizations are typical anti-predator behaviors.

No plants or fungi are visible — the environment is abiotic (ice, snow, rock). No algae or microbial mats are discernible.

---

### **4. Object and Person Tracking**

- **Sea Otter**: Single individual, only in intro (0:00–0:04). Not part of main ecological scene.
- **Emperor Penguin Chicks**: Same cohort tracked across scenes. Estimated **12–20 individuals** total across frames, with ~10–12 consistently in medium/close shots. Individual identification is difficult due to similarity, but movements suggest continuity (e.g., same chick falls at 0:21 and reappears later).
- **Southern Giant Petrel**: One individual tracked throughout — same plumage, bill shape, behavior. No duplication.
- **Adélie Penguin**: One clearly tracked walking past; others in background are unconfirmed.

No humans, equipment, or artificial objects (except watermark/logo overlays) are visible in the field footage.

---

## ✅ Final Species Inventory & Summary

| # | Species | Scientific Name | Life Stage | Approx. Count | Notes |
|---|---------|------------------|------------|---------------|-------|
| 1 | Sea Otter | *Enhydra lutris* | Adult | 1 | Intro only; not ecologically linked to main footage. |
| 2 | Emperor Penguin | *Aptenodytes forsteri* | Juvenile (chicks, downy) | 12–20 (observable) | Primary subjects; form crèche; exhibit anti-predator behavior. |
| 3 | Southern Giant Petrel | *Macronectes giganteus* | Juvenile/subadult | 1 | Repeated interactions with chicks; attempted predation. |
| 4 | Adélie Penguin | *Pygoscelis adeliae* | Adult | ≥1 (1 confirmed, 1–2 possible in bg) | Brief passerby; no interaction. |

### 🚫 Absent / Not Identified:
- No skuas (though often associate with penguin colonies — none clearly visible).
- No Weddell seals, leopard seals, or other mammals.
- No vascular plants, mosses, lichens, or phytoplankton visible.
- No insects or invertebrates.

---

## Conclusion

The video clearly documents **four distinct animal species**, though only **three** are ecologically interacting in the Antarctic setting (Emperor penguin chicks, Southern Giant Petrel, and Adélie penguin). The sea otter is a non-contextual intro element.

The most significant biological observation is the natural predatory/scavenging behavior of the Southern Giant Petrel toward vulnerable Emperor penguin chicks — a well-documented but rarely captured interaction in such detail.
